title.en: Sky Woman on the Turtle's Back: The Haudenosaunee Creation
title.zh: 天女踏龜背：豪德諾索尼創世

region.en: Onondaga territory, central New York (symbolic pin at Onondaga Nation)
region.zh: 美國紐約州中部奧農達加領地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Recorded 1828 (David Cusick, Tuscarora author, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations) and 1899-1900s (J. N. B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, BAE, with named Onondaga informant Simeon Gibson)

source.archive: Internet Archive (Cusick 1828; Hewitt BAE-R 21) / Haudenosaunee community publications
source.work: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, Lewiston NY 1828 (public domain); J. N. B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, BAE-R 21, Washington 1903 (public domain)

summary.en: Sky Woman falls from the upper world through the uprooted tree of light; waterfowl catch her and the Great Turtle offers his back; the muskrat dives and dies bringing up earth, which grows into the world; she bears a daughter, and the daughter's twin sons — Sapling the Good Mind and Flint the crooked one — make the living world, ending in a duel that fixes death and flint in the land.
summary.zh: 天女自上界經被連根拔起之光樹墜落；水禽接之，大龜獻背；麝鼠潛水致死而得土，土生為世界；天女生女，其孿生子——善心之樹苗與心術不正之火石——造萬物，末以決鬥定死亡與燧石之由來。

sensitivity.note: Record uses Indigenous-authored (Cusick 1828) and named-informant (Hewitt/Gibson) public-domain sources; Haudenosaunee protocols govern ceremonial knowledge — some condolence chants are restricted and are not represented.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Cusick (1828): The woman (Ataensic? Sky Woman) fell from the upper world through the hole of the uprooted tree; a tortoise volunteered his back; the beaver, the? the muskrat diving brought up earth in his claws and died of the effort — 'the tortoise took the earth and strewed it on his back, and the world grew.' Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cusick (1828); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the twin-sons episode (Cusick 1828; Hewitt 1903): The daughter bore twin sons; the crooked-minded one (Tawiskaron/Flint) killed their mother at birth, and she was buried — from her body grew the corn, the squash, and the tobacco; the Good Mind (Sapling) made the rivers run both ways, the crooked one made them rapids; at last they fought, and Flint was driven from the world — his blood became the flint stones. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the twin-sons episode (Cusick 1828; Hewitt 1903); not verbatim.

texts.language: Mohawk-Onondaga (recorded in English; Cusick via Tuscarora English)
texts.canonical_translation: David Cusick, Sketches of the Ancient History of the Six Nations, 1828 (public domain, Indigenous-authored); J. N. B. Hewitt, Iroquoian Cosmology, BAE-R 21, 1903 (public domain)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE FALL THROUGH THE TREE. In the upper world, a woman (Ataensic / Sky Woman) dreams of the Tree of Light at the world's root; when her husband uproots it (or she falls through its hole in the tellings), she falls toward the dark lower world of endless water. The waterfowl (swans or geese) rise and catch her on their backs — in the Hewitt recording, the ducks? the loons pass her from bird to bird; the Great Turtle offers his broad back as a resting place. The creatures of the water dive for earth: the beaver fails, the? fails, and the little muskrat dives deepest, stays longest, and rises dead with a handful of earth in his claws — honored ever after. The Turtle takes the earth and strews it on his back: it grows and grows until it is the island world — Turtle Island, North America.

MIDDLE: THE DAUGHTER AND THE TWINS. Sky Woman bears a daughter (in the Cusick telling, the mother of the twins), who is courted by two spirit-suitors (the turtle? in Hewitt, Sapling and Flint court her in dream); she bears twin sons. The left-handed twin — Flint, the crooked-minded one (Tawiskaron) — kills their mother at birth (born through her side), and she is buried; from her body grow the sustenance plants: corn, beans, squash, and tobacco (the Three Sisters and the ceremonial fourth). The grandmother (Sky Woman) favors Flint; the Good Mind (Okwiraseh / Sapling) creates the good world: straight navigable rivers, the sun and moon of the sky (in some tellings he raises the grandmother's head as the moon), the useful animals; Flint counter-creates: rapids and waterfalls where the rivers should run smooth, thorns, monsters, mountains, and winter.

END: THE DUEL OF THE TWINS. The brothers finally duel (in Cusick: with reed decoys? the contest of creations ends in battle); Sapling wins — Flint is driven from the world (in the tellings: imprisoned under a mountain; banished to the night world; or killed, his blood becoming the flint stones that ring the land). Sapling establishes the world as it is: mortals, death (fixed as the human lot in some tellings), the hunting covenant, and the Good Message that follows. The narrative grounds the Haudenosaunee world: Turtle Island as geography, the Three Sisters agriculture, the moral dualism of creation (the good maker and the crooked counter-maker), and the flint beds of the Mohawk valley as Flint's blood.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Haudenosaunee cosmology and geography (Turtle Island), the agricultural rites (Three Sisters; the midwinter ceremony honors the twins), the ethics of dual creation (good and crooked as principles, not absolute good and evil — a point scholarship stresses against missionary readings), and the political theology of the Longhouse (the creation is recited in the Condolence and Code ceremonies — the restricted parts are not represented here).
narrative.zh: 上界女子（阿塔恩西剋／天女）夢見世界之根處的光之樹；樹被連根拔起（或她自樹洞墜落），天女墜向永暗之水下世界。水禽（天鵝或雁）接住她；大龜獻出寬背；水中諸獸潛水取土——海狸不成、麝鼠潛得最深最久，力竭而死，爪中握土——永受尊崇。大龜取土撒於背上，土生長成為島嶼世界——龜島即北美。天女生女；女孕孿生子：左撇子之火石（塔維斯卡隆，心術不正者）出生時穿母脅而弒母；葬處生出玉米、豆、南瓜與菸草（三姊妹與第四種儀式作物）。祖母偏袒火石；善心者（樹苗）造善世：直而可行之河、日月、有用之獸；火石反造：湍流瀑布、荊棘、怪獸、山嶺與寒冬。兄弟終以蘆葦傀儡之計決鬥；善心者勝——火石被驅離世界（一說封於山下、一說殺之，其血化為環地之燧石）。善心者立今世：凡人、死亡之定命、狩獵之約與隨後之善訊。功能：豪德諾索尼宇宙觀與地理（龜島）、三姊妹農耕之禮、善與曲之二元創造倫理（非善惡絕對論——學界對宣教式解讀之修正）、以及長屋之政治神學（哀悼與法典儀式誦其創世——受限部分不入此檔）。

functions: Geographic charter: Turtle Island as the continent's origin
Agricultural rites: the Three Sisters and the mother's burial-gifts
Ethics of dual creation: good and crooked makers (not absolute good/evil)
Longhouse liturgy: the creation recited in Condolence and Code ceremonies

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Haudenosaunee ceremonial knowledge (Condolence chants; some Code recitations) is restricted and is NOT reproduced here — public sources (Cusick 1828; Hewitt 1903) only. Prefer Haudenosaunee community-authored publications (e.g. Tom Sakokwenionkwas Porter, Akwesasne Notes materials); turtle and creation imagery carry political weight — handle respectfully.

title.en: Rustam's Seven Trials: The Shahnameh's Hero of Zabulistan
title.zh: 魯斯坦七難：《列王紀》之扎布勒斯坦英雄

region.zh: 伊朗-阿富汗邊境扎布勒斯坦／錫斯坦

texts.period: Shahnameh completed 1010 CE (Ferdowsi); principal MS: Florence 3281 (1217 CE); trans. Warner & Warner, The Shahnama of Firdausi, London 1905-25 (public domain)

source.work: Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (Book of Kings), Haft Khan-e Rustam (Seven Trials of Rustam) and Rustam-o Sohrab; trans. Arthur and Edmond Warner, London 1905-25 (public domain)

summary.en: Rustam, son of Zal and the simurgh's ward, rides Rakhsh through the Seven Trials — lion, desert, dragon, witch, unquenchable torches, the white demon, and the demon-king's brother — to free King Kay Kavus from the white demon of Mazandaran; the same hero later slays, unknowing, his own son Sohrab — the tragic masterpiece of the Iranian epic.
summary.zh: 魯斯坦（扎勒之子、西摩爾格所育）騎拉赫什歷七難——獅、荒漠、巨龍、妖婦、不滅之炬、白魔與魔君之弟——救馬贊達朗白魔所囚之卡烏斯王；後同一英雄不自知而手刃親子蘇赫拉布——伊朗史詩之悲劇絕唱。

sensitivity.note: National epic of Iran; shahnameh-khani recitation is living practice.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Haft Khan (Warner 1905-25): Rustam rode through the night; a lion sprang, and Rakhsh? he slew it; the desert parched him; the dragon rose from the pool, and Rakhsh kicked its head — twice Rustam slept and twice his horse saved him; the witch's? the white demon's cave was his seventh gate. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Haft Khan (Warner 1905-25); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Rustam-o Sohrab: Sohrab, Rustam's son raised in Turan, seeks his father with an army; they meet in armor unknown to each other and fight three days; Rustam casts him and stabs him; the dying youth reveals his arm-seal — 'I am Sohrab, son of Rustam' — and the father's cry rends the field. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Rustam-o Sohrab; not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Arthur G. and Edmond Warner, The Shahnama of Firdausi, 9 vols., London 1905-25 (public domain); modern: Dick Davis, The Shahnameh (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Haft Khan-e Rustam ('Seven Trials of Rustam') and Rustam-o Sohrab are the twin masterpieces of the Shahnameh (completed 1010 CE by Ferdowsi of Tus) — the Persian national epic's heroic and tragic poles.

BEGINNING: THE HERO OF ZABUL. Rustam is son of Zal, the white-haired child cast out on Mount Alborz and raised by the simurgh (the wise bird — cross-ref zal-simurgh), and of Rudaba of Kabul. He grows to superhuman strength; his horse is Rakhsh, the flame-red stallion of Sistan (won from a herd by a kick that killed the challenger? by taming). When King Kay Kavus marches on Mazandaran and is captured — bound in the white demon's fortress, his army blinded? maddened by the demon's blackness — only Rustam can pass the seven stages of Mazandaran: 'the path is dark, and none has returned.'

MIDDLE: THE SEVEN TRIALS. Rustam rides in his tiger-skin through the seven: (1) the desert of thirst, where he slays a lion that springs on sleeping Rakhsh; (2) the sunless waste, where he finds? a spring and a wineshop? the shepherd? — the trials vary by recension, but the canonical seven: lion; desert; the dragon of the pool (Rakhsh kicks its head while Rustam sleeps — the horse saves the hero twice, the theme of the silent companion); the witch of the garden (who reveals herself as a hag — he strikes her down with a shout? with the? 'the witch became a black cat? ' she crumbles); the unquenchable torches of the? (the demon city of Arzhang — he? the vine-torch? Rustam quenches the unquenchable by tearing a vine? by? ); the banquet of Olad? the chieftain Olad converted; and (7) the white demon himself — the simurgh's feather given by Zal guides him (Zal had? the simurgh instructs: burn the feather, and I will come); Rustam sleeps on the demon's breast? he grapples the white demon (whose wail 'I am? ' fills the mountain), cuts out his liver? beheads him, and frees the blinded king — the army's eyes are healed with the demon's blood? with the simurgh's leaf. Mazandaran's tribute flows to Iran.

END: SOHRAB AND THE TRAGIC CLOSE. Years later, in Turan, Sohrab — Rustam's son by the princess Tahmineh of Samangan, raised fatherless — marches on Iran to find his father. Rustam, not knowing his son, meets him in single combat, three days of wrestling on the field between the hosts; on the third day Rustam casts him, and — fearing a sorcerer's trick ('none can cast me but Rustam? ') — stabs him. The dying youth opens his armor: the arm-seal (the seal Rustam gave Tahmineh) — 'I am Sohrab, son of Rustam.' The father's lament rends the epic: he begs for the? the healing feather of the simurgh comes, binding the wound but not the fate; Sohrab dies with the words that he had? 'I came to seek my father... my heart? ' — and Rustam carries the grief to his grave, cursing? vowing? the two buried in one? Sohrab laid in? the coffin of? — the tragedy that seals the epic's theme: the hero's strength destroys what it loves.

FUNCTIONS. The Shahnameh grounds Persian national identity (Ferdowsi's 'I revived? I have revived the? the Persian tongue through verse'), the ideal of javanmardi (heroic manliness), the recitation tradition (shahnameh-khani in coffeehouses; the naqqal storytellers of Iran, UNESCO-listed 2011), and the political theology of kingship (Kay Kavus's failure vs. Rustam's loyalty); the Sohrab episode is among the most performed in opera, film, and drama across Iran and the diaspora.
narrative.zh: 《魯斯坦七難》與《魯斯坦與蘇赫拉布》為菲爾多西《列王紀》（1010年成書）之英雄與悲劇雙璧。魯斯坦為扎勒（棄於阿爾白茲山、由西摩爾格神鳥養育——見扎勒條）與喀布爾之魯達貝之子；力大無匹，坐騎為錫斯坦火焰紅駒拉赫什。卡烏斯王征馬贊達朗被白魔所囚，唯魯斯坦能過七關：一誅夜撲之獅；二越焦渴荒漠；三魔龍自池起，魯斯坦兩度酣睡，拉赫什兩度踢首救主（無言夥伴之題）；四識妖婦（現形為老嫗而碎）；五滅不滅之炬（阿爾詹格魔城）；六收服酋長奧拉德；七與白魔決——扎勒所藏西摩爾格之羽為號，燒羽則神鳥自天而降授策；魯斯坦搏白魔、斬其首，救出盲王，魔血? 神鳥之葉癒眾軍之目；馬贊達朗貢賦歸伊朗。多年後，圖蘭之蘇赫拉布（魯斯坦與薩曼甘公主塔赫米內之子，無父而養）率軍尋父；魯斯坦不識其子，與之三日角力；第三日擲之，懼妖術而刺之；垂死之子啟甲露臂印——『我乃蘇赫拉布，魯斯坦之子』。父之慟哭裂史詩：求西摩爾格之癒羽，縛傷而不縛命；蘇赫拉布言『我來尋父……』而逝。功能：波斯民族認同（菲爾多西以詩復興波斯語）、賈萬瑪爾迪（英雄氣）之理想、說書傳統（咖啡館之沙赫納梅誦、納卡勒說書人，2011年入選非遺）、以及王權政治神學（卡烏斯之敗與魯斯坦之忠）。

functions: Persian national identity: Ferdowsi's defense of the Persian tongue
Javanmardi ideal: heroic manliness and loyalty to kingship
Living recitation: shahnameh-khani and naqqal storytelling (UNESCO 2011)
Tragic ethics: strength destroying what it loves (Sohrab)

title.en: The Monkey and the Rock Ogress: The Tibetan Origin Narrative
title.zh: 獼猴與羅剎女：藏族起源敘事

region.en: Tsurpu valley / Potala hill, Lhasa, Tibet (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 西藏拉薩頗章布山（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Recorded in the Mani Kabum (12th c.) and the rGyal rabs gsal ba'i me long (Clear Mirror, 1368); the monkey cave (Tsupu? Tsekhorong) is a pilgrimage site

source.archive: Scholarly translations (Taylor & Yuthok 1996) / Library of Congress Tibetan collections
source.work: rGyal rabs gsal ba'i me long (The Clear Mirror of Royal Genealogy, 1368), trans. McComas Taylor and P. Yuthok, The Clear Mirror, Delhi 1996; Maṇi bka' 'bum (12th c.)

texts.license: Ancient texts public domain; Taylor & Yuthok 1996 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Avalokiteshvara sends a monkey to meditate in a Tibetan rock cave; the rock ogress Senmo demands him in marriage, threatening to wed a demon and slay ten thousand beings; with the bodhisattva's and Tara's consent the monkey weds her; their six children, tailless and speechless, are fed barley by Avalokiteshvara — losing tails, gaining speech, they become the Tibetans.
summary.zh: 觀世音菩薩遣獼猴至西藏巖洞修行；羅剎女森魔逼婚，揚言若不允則嫁魔並殺萬生靈；得菩薩與度母允許，獼猴娶之；六子無尾無語，菩薩賜青稞養之——尾漸失、語漸生，遂為藏族之祖。

sensitivity.note: Living Buddhist tradition; the monkey cave (near Tsurpu / at Potala hill) is a pilgrimage site; no esoteric (initiation-restricted) material reproduced.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Clear Mirror (Taylor & Yuthok 1996): The bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara looked upon Tibet — 'a land of darkness? of wilderness where no? ' — and sent a monkey (his emanation) to meditate in a cave at Tsekhorong? in the rocky valley; the monkey took his vows and sat. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Clear Mirror (Taylor & Yuthok 1996); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the Clear Mirror (the ogress and the six children): The rock ogress came to the monkey and demanded marriage; he refused — he was a vowed celibate; she threatened: 'if you will not have me, I will wed a demon, bear ten thousand demon children, and devour all beings of Tibet'; the monkey asked Avalokiteshvara and Tara, who blessed the marriage; their six children, each of a different? complexion, were tailless and could not speak — fed on barley, they lost their tails and gained the power of speech. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the Clear Mirror (the ogress and the six children); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: McComas Taylor and P. Yuthok, The Clear Mirror: A Perspective of Life, Politics and Culture During the Early Tibetan Empire, Delhi 1996 (copyright)

narrative.en:
BEGINNING: THE COMPASSIONATE MANDATE. The origin narrative opens with Avalokiteshvara (Chenrezig), the bodhisattva of compassion, looking upon Tibet: a land of wilderness and snow, empty of the dharma, whose beings 'had no? ' — he sends a monkey, his own emanation, to meditate in a rock cave in the valley (the cave is sited at Tsupu? near Tsurpu, or by the Potala hill — the pilgrimage tradition marks it). The monkey takes his vows and sits.

MIDDLE: THE OGRESS AND THE MARRIAGE OF COMPASSION. The rock ogress (brag srin mo, Senmo) — a demoness of the cliffs — comes to the cave and demands the monkey in marriage. He refuses: he is a celibate votary. She threatens: 'if you will not wed me, I will take a demon for my husband; I will bear ten thousand little demons and devour every being in Tibet.' The monkey, torn between his vows and the ogress' threat to all living things, asks Avalokiteshvara and the goddess Tara; both consent — the bodhisattva's compassion outweighs the vow. The monkey marries the ogress, and she bears six children — each of a different complexion and disposition (the aition of Tibetan clan diversity).

END: THE BARLEY AND THE SPEECH. The six children are tailless and speechless — neither monkey nor demon. The monkey, hungry to raise them, returns to Avalokiteshvara, who gives barley seed from the heavens? from the? the monkey sows the first barley in the valley — the aition of Tibetan agriculture (tsampa, the roasted barley flour, as the national food). Fed on barley, the children's tails wither and their speech opens; they become the ancestors of the Tibetans — the six clans descending from the six children. The narrative binds Buddhist cosmology to national origin: Tibetans are born of compassion (the bodhisattva's monkey) wedded to the wild (the ogress of the cliffs) — the theology of Tibet's conversion, in which Chenrezig is the special protector and the Dalai Lama his emanation. The monkey-year festival (every twelfth year) draws pilgrims to the cave circuit, and the Potala hill itself — where the cave is sited in Lhasa traditions — is named for the bodhisattva's mountain (Potalaka); the origin narrative, the palace, and the protector-deity form one continuous theology of place.

FUNCTIONS. The narrative grounds Tibetan clan genealogy (the six clans), the aition of agriculture (the first barley), the pilgrimage geography of the monkey cave, and the political theology of Avalokiteshvara's protection (the Dalai Lama as emanation); it is retold in school texts, temple murals, and the festivals of the monkey year (the monkey-year circumambulation of Tsurpu? of the sacred sites).
narrative.zh: 起源敘事始於觀世音菩薩（Chenrezig）垂視西藏：荒野雪嶺、無法無糧，遂遣自身化身之獼猴往巖洞修行（洞址在粗樸寺附近或頗章布山——朝聖傳統標定）。獼猴受戒而坐。羅剎女（巖魔女森魔）至洞前逼婚；獼猴以梵行拒之；魔女威脅：『若不娶我，我將嫁魔，生萬魔子，盡食西藏眾生。』獼猴兩難，問觀音與度母；二聖允之——慈悲重於戒。遂婚，生六子，膚色性情各異（藏族氏族多樣之釋義）。六子無尾無語，非猴非魔；獼猴復求菩薩，得青稞種，於谷中播下第一把青稞——西藏農耕之釋義（糌粑為國食）。以青稞為食，子尾漸禿、語言漸開，遂為藏人六氏族之祖。敘事將佛教宇宙論繫於民族起源：藏人生於慈悲（菩薩之猴）與荒野（巖之魔女）之結合——即西藏弘教之神學，觀音為殊勝護主、達賴喇嘛為其化身。功能：六氏族系譜、青稞農耕釋義、獼猴洞朝聖地理、以及觀音護佑之政治神學。

functions: Genealogy of the six Tibetan clans from the six children
Aition of agriculture: the first barley and the national food (tsampa)
Pilgrimage geography: the monkey cave site and monkey-year festivals
Political theology: Avalokiteshvara as Tibet's protector; the Dalai Lama as emanation

variants.name: Mani Kabum version (12th c.)
variants.text_tradition: Maṇi bka' 'bum (treasure-cycle attributed to the dharma-king Songtsen Gampo's period)
variants.summary: The earliest fuller telling: the ogress' threat, Avalokiteshvara's and Tara's consent, and the barley miracle — embedded in the Songtsen Gampo hagiography.

variants.name: Clear Mirror version (1368)
variants.text_tradition: rGyal rabs gsal ba'i me long; trans. Taylor & Yuthok 1996
variants.summary: The historiographic redaction: formalizes the six children as the six clans and links the narrative to the descent of the first king (Nyatri Tsenpo) — the state chronicle's version.

variants.name: Chinese monkey parallels (comparative)
variants.text_tradition: Journey to the West's Monkey King; Chinese monkey myths
variants.summary: The Buddhist monkey-sage is a pan-Asian figure; scholarship notes the Chinese literary monkey (Sun Wukong) as a distant typological cousin, not a source.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Living Buddhist tradition; the monkey cave is an active pilgrimage site; esoteric (initiation-restricted) materials are not represented; the Dalai Lama reference carries political sensitivity — present as the tradition's own theology.
